concepts.name: Non-SARGable predicates: functions and conversions on indexed columns
The satisfies operator vs type annotations in TypeScript
TanStack Query key design and prefix invalidation

questions.prompt: `Orders` has a nonclustered index on `OrderDate`, yet `SELECT OrderId FROM Orders WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025` scans the whole index on SQL Server and burns CPU. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Add `OrderDate` to the index's INCLUDE list so the query is fully covered
Add `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` so the optimizer sees the literal year every time
Rewrite it as `OrderDate >= '2025-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2026-01-01'`
Rebuild the index and update its statistics so the optimizer trusts it

questions.explanation: Wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server must compute `YEAR()` for every row before it can compare, so it scans. A half-open date range leaves the column bare, so the index can seek. Covering the query doesn't help while the predicate still can't seek, `RECOMPILE` fixes parameter-sensitive plans rather than function-wrapped columns, and fresh statistics don't make a function seekable.

sources.title: Troubleshoot High CPU Usage Issues in SQL Server
sources.claim: Applying any function or computation to a column in a search predicate generally makes it non-SARGable and forces a scan; the fix is to rewrite the predicate so the column stands alone (or index a computed column), and CONVERT/CAST or implicit conversions on the column have the same effect.

sources.title: Date and Time conditions causing SQL performance problems
sources.claim: Functions such as TRUNC on a date column are black boxes that stop a plain index on the column being used; write continuous periods as an explicit range condition (>= start AND < next period), even for a single day.

choices.text: It skips the excess property check, so a typo like `bleu` is not reported
It casts the object like `as` does, so values of a wrong type are accepted
It checks the object at runtime and throws if a key of `Colors` is missing
`palette.green` stays `string`, so `palette.green.toUpperCase()` compiles

questions.explanation: `satisfies` checks the object against the type, so a misspelt key or a wrong value type is still an error, but the variable keeps its own, more specific inferred type. With the annotation, `palette.green` is `string | number[]` and `.toUpperCase()` fails to compile. It is a compile-time check only: no cast and no runtime code.

sources.title: TypeScript 4.9
sources.claim: The satisfies operator checks that an expression matches a type (catching typos such as `bleu` and wrong value types) while keeping the expression's most specific inferred type, so `palette.green.toUpperCase()` still compiles; a type annotation instead widens `palette.green` to `string | RGB`.

questions.prompt: A React orders page uses TanStack Query with `queryKey: ['orders']` and a `queryFn` that fetches `/api/orders?status=${status}&page=${page}`. Users see the wrong page's orders after changing filters, and the list stays stale after they create an order. How would you design the query keys and the invalidation?

model_answer.summary: Put every variable the query function uses into the key, such as `['orders', { status, page }]`, so each combination is cached and refetched on its own, and after the mutation invalidate by the shared prefix `['orders']`.
key_points: Every variable the `queryFn` depends on (here `status` and `page`) belongs in the query key; with the fixed key `['orders']` all filters share one cache entry and changing a filter doesn't refetch
With the variables in the key, each combination is cached separately and a change of variable triggers a fetch automatically
Keys are hashed deterministically: the order of keys inside an object doesn't matter, but the order of array items does, so keep one stable shape such as `['orders', { status, page }]`

After creating an order, call `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] })`: it matches every key starting with `orders`, marks them stale and refetches the ones on screen (`exact: true` would target only one key)

questions.explanation: A query key is the cache's identity for the data, so it must change whenever the request changes. Treating the key as a fixed label is the tempting mistake: the cache then serves one filter's data for another. Prefix matching lets one invalidation refresh every page and filter of the list after a write.

sources.title: Query Keys
sources.claim: If the query function depends on a variable, include it in the query key so queries are cached independently and refetched when the variable changes; keys are hashed deterministically, object key order doesn't matter, but array item order does.

sources.title: Query Invalidation
sources.claim: invalidateQueries marks matching queries stale (overriding staleTime) and refetches those currently rendered; `{ queryKey: ['todos'] }` matches every key starting with `todos`, and `exact: true` restricts it to that exact key.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, `users.email` has a plain B-tree index, and the login query runs `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)`. The plan is a sequential scan. Which change lets this query use an index without rewriting it?

choices.text: Create a hash index on `email`, since hash indexes are built for equality
Index the expression itself: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))`
Run `ANALYZE users` so the planner learns how selective `email` really is
Change the column to `citext` in the query only, by casting `email::citext`

questions.explanation: An index on `email` stores `email` values, not `lower(email)`, so a predicate on `lower(email)` can't use it. PostgreSQL can index the expression itself; the cost is computing it on every insert and update, which pays off when reads matter more. A different index type or fresh statistics still index the bare column, and a cast in the query is another expression the index doesn't match. On SQL Server the equivalent is an indexed computed column.

sources.title: 11.7. Indexes on Expressions
sources.claim: WHERE lower(col1) = 'value' can use an index only if one is defined on lower(col1); index expressions are computed on every insert and non-HOT update, so they suit workloads where retrieval speed matters more than write speed.

questions.prompt: `const routes = { home: "/", orders: "/orders" } satisfies Record<string, string>;` What is `keyof typeof routes`?

choices.text: `string`, because the `Record<string, string>` type replaces the inferred type
`never`, because `satisfies` only checks the value and keeps no type for it
`"home" | "orders"`, because `satisfies` keeps the object's inferred type
`string | number`, because an index signature's keys include numbers too

questions.explanation: `satisfies` validates the object against `Record<string, string>` but leaves `routes` with its inferred type, `{ home: string; orders: string }`, so its keys are the literal names. That is why it suits config objects: you keep autocomplete and typo checks on `routes.orders`. Annotating the variable with `Record<string, string>` instead would give it the index signature's keys and lose the names.

questions.prompt: After a mutation you call `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })`. The cache holds `['todos']`, `['todos', { page: 1 }]` and `['todo', 5]`. Which queries are invalidated?

choices.text: Only `['todos']`, since query key matching is exact unless you opt out of it
`['todos']` and `['todos', { page: 1 }]`, since the key matches as a prefix
All three, because `['todo', 5]` shares the `todo` stem with the given key
None until `refetchQueries` runs, since invalidation only lowers `staleTime`

questions.explanation: `invalidateQueries` matches every query whose key starts with the given key, so both `todos` queries are marked stale and refetched if on screen. `exact: true` would limit it to `['todos']` alone. Key items are compared whole, so `'todo'` is not a prefix match for `'todos'`. Invalidation itself marks the queries stale and refetches active ones; no separate call is needed.

sources.title: Query Invalidation

questions.prompt: A React orders page uses TanStack Query with `queryKey: ['orders']` and a `queryFn` that fetches `/api/orders?status=${status}&page=${page}`. Users see the wrong page after changing filters, and the list stays stale after creating an order. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `status` and `page` belong in the key, such as `['orders', { status, page }]`
`invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] })` matches every key starting with `orders`
`{ status, page }` and `{ page, status }` hash to the same query key
`['orders', status, page]` and `['orders', page, status]` hash to the same key
Invalidation only marks queries stale; nothing refetches until the next mount

questions.explanation: Every variable the query function uses must be in the key; with the fixed key `['orders']` all filters share one cache entry, so changing a filter doesn't refetch. Keys hash deterministically: the order of properties inside an object doesn't matter, but the order of array items does. After the mutation, `invalidateQueries` with `['orders']` prefix-matches keys such as `['orders', { status, page }]`, marks them stale and refetches the ones being rendered right away; `exact: true` would narrow it to one key.

sources.title: Query Keys
sources.claim: Query keys must include every variable the query function uses that changes; keys are hashed deterministically, so the order of keys in an object doesn't matter but the order of array items does.

sources.title: Query Invalidation
sources.claim: invalidateQueries marks matching queries stale and refetches those currently rendered; a key such as ['todos'] matches every key that starts with it, and exact: true restricts it to an exact match.
